statement: Some people believe that spending money on space exploration is a waste when there are so many problems on Earth. Others argue that space research brings important benefits to humanity.
question: Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
model:
Each time a rocket is launched at a cost of billions, critics ask whether the money might have been better spent on hospitals or schools. Although this objection is understandable, I am convinced that space research repays its cost many times over and deserves continued public support.

The case against such spending rests on a simple moral comparison. While hundreds of millions of people lack clean drinking water and basic healthcare, sending probes to distant planets can appear an indulgence for wealthy nations. Opponents also point out that some recent missions have been driven as much by national prestige or the ambitions of private billionaires as by any scientific purpose, and they argue that urgent problems such as climate change demand every available resource.

Yet this argument overlooks how much of everyday life already depends on space research. Satellites provide the weather forecasts that warn farmers of droughts and coastal towns of approaching hurricanes, as well as the navigation systems used by every delivery driver and ambulance crew. Technologies developed for astronauts, including water purification systems, scratch-resistant lenses and improved medical imaging, have found their way into ordinary homes and hospitals. Ironically, it is satellite monitoring that has given scientists the most precise measurements of melting ice sheets and deforestation, the very evidence needed to tackle environmental crises on Earth.

Moreover, the sums involved are smaller than commonly assumed. The budget of NASA, for example, amounts to less than half of one per cent of American federal spending, a fraction of what is spent on defence. Cancelling space programmes would therefore do little to solve poverty, while sacrificing knowledge and innovation with long-term benefits.

In conclusion, while the needs of people on Earth must remain a priority, they are not in genuine competition with space exploration. Properly directed, space research is an investment in solving terrestrial problems rather than a distraction from them.
